catalog_quote: 1.9.1. सार्थक बलाघात शब्द स्तर पर ही- मानक हिन्दी और बांगरू दोनों में सार्थक बलाघात की सत्ता शब्द स्तर पर है अर्थात् वाक्य में किसी शब्द पर बलाघात का स्वनिम होने या न होने से तो अर्थ भेद हो जाता है परन्तु शब्द में किसी अक्षर पर बलाघात कम है या अधिक, इस बात से अन्तर नहीं पड़ता। [...] 1.9.2. अक्षर स्तर पर बलाघात अनुमेय :- सामान्यता शब्द में केवल एक अक्षर पर ही बलाघात होता है और मानक हिन्दी और बांगरू दोनों में ही यह अनुमेय होता है। शब्द के विभिन्न अक्षरों में से किस अक्षर पर अनुमेय बलाघात होगा, इस सम्बन्ध में विद्वानों द्वारा जो विचार मानक हिन्दी के बारे में प्रकट किये गये हैं, वे ही बांगरू के अनुमेय बलाघात पर भी लागू होते हैं। 1.9.3. अक्षर स्तरीय बलाघात का प्रभाव: मानक हिन्दी की अपेक्षा बांगरू में अनुमेय बलाघात अपेक्षाकृत सबल होता है। बांगरू में ऐसी सबलता के कारण बलाघातित अक्षर का स्वरूप मानक हिन्दी के तदनुरूपी अक्षर की अपेक्षा कुछ भारी हो जाता है और बलाघातित अक्षर से पूर्ववर्ती अक्षर का स्वरूप मानक हिन्दी की अपेक्षा कुछ हल्का हो जाता है। [...] (4) मानक हिन्दी का बलाघात रहित अक्षर यदि दीर्घ स्वर वाला मुक्त अक्षर हो तो तदनुरूपी बांगरू अक्षर में स्वर का ह्रस्वीकरण हो जाता है। [...] /बाजार/ /बजार/ [...] /बीमार/ /बिमार/ [...] /तूफान/ /तुफान/ [...] (5) मानक हिन्दी में बलाघातित अक्षर से पूर्ववर्ती अक्षर यदि केवल ह्रस्व स्वर हो तो बांगरू उच्चारण में ऐसे बलाघात रहित अक्षर का लोप हो जाता है। [...] /अनाज/ /नाज/ /अहीर/ /हीर/

new_statements.translation: In both Standard Hindi and Bangru, meaningful stress exists at the word level, i.e. whether or not the stress phoneme falls on a given word in a sentence does change the meaning, but whether the stress on a given syllable within a word is weaker or stronger makes no difference. [...] Normally only one syllable in a word bears stress, and in both Standard Hindi and Bangru this is predictable. As to which of the various syllables of a word will bear the predictable stress, the views scholars have expressed about Standard Hindi apply equally to the predictable stress of Bangru.
new_statements.citation: Bansal, Somdatt (सोमदत्त बंसल). 1981. Mānak Hindī aur Bāṅgrū kā vyatirekī adhyayan [A contrastive analysis of Standard Hindi and Bangru]. PhD thesis, Panjab University, Chandigarh. Ch. 1 Svanaprakriyā, §1.9 Balāghāt, §1.9.1-1.9.2, pp. 95-96.
new_statements.locator: §1.9.1 'sārthak balāghāt śabd star par hī' p. 95 and §1.9.2 'akṣar star par balāghāt anumey' p. 96 (pp. 117-118); Bangru suprasegmental inventory and note 2 quoting Jag Deva Singh on p. 14 (p. 36)
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the page scan and printed pp. 95-96 of the archive.org scan; archive.org item manak-hindi-aur-bangru-ka-vyatireki-adhyayan confirmed live via its metadata endpoint). Section 1.9 balaghat with subsections 1.9.1 'sarthak balaghat shabd star par hi' (p. 95) and 1.9.2 'akshar star par balaghat anumey' (p. 96) is there, and the two quoted passages read as reported. Minor differences only: the typescript has 'samanyata' where the report normalises to 'samanyataya', writes 'bangru' with anusvara rather than chandrabindu, and carries footnote superscripts (1 after 'shabd star', 4 after 'vidvanon') that the report omits. Footnote 4 on p. 96 is 'Sharma, Aryendra; A Basic Grammar of Modern Hind…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive: one syllable per word is stressed and its position is predictable (anumey). Bansal does not restate the placement rule; he says it is the same as the rule scholars give for Standard Hindi (footnote 4 cites Aryendra Sharma 1975, A Basic Grammar of Modern Hindi, pp. 17-18), which in that literature is the syllable-weight rule (stress the heaviest syllable; among equals the rightmost non-final). The 'weight-sensitive' reading is therefore by reference to Hindi, not from a rule spelled out for Bangru; treat as medium confidence. §1.9.3 adds that Bangru's predictable stress is stronger than Hindi's: the stressed syllable becomes heavier (short stressed vowel lengthens, open stressed syllable closes by gemination, e.g. Hindi /moṭā/ vs Bangru /moṭṭā/) and the pre-tonic syllable lighter (unstressed long vowels shorten, initial pretonic short vowels drop), pp. 96-98.
new_statements.exceptions: Bansal rejects syllable-level minimal pairs claimed for Hindi (Mehrotra 1970 /ˈmanā/ vs /maˈnā/; Arun 1961 /ˈgalā/ vs /gaˈlā/, /ˈghaṭā/ vs /ghaˈṭā/) as non-distinctive for both languages (p. 96). The same thesis (p. 14 n. 2-3) quotes Jag Deva Singh (1962-63): stress is not a phoneme in Bangru, but is used for emphasis; Bansal keeps a stress phoneme only for that word-level emphatic function.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (śabd star): stress is distinctive only as sentence emphasis on a word; within the word it is predictable and non-contrastive. Bansal's data are the Bangru of Jind (author's mother tongue), compared with Standard Hindi; no citation-form vs connected-speech distinction is drawn. Sharma 1968 (Central Haryanvi of Meham) lists pitch, terminal contour, juncture and nasality as the suprasegmental phonemes and no stress phoneme, consistent with Bansal.
new_statements.identity_note: Bansal 1981 describes Bangru (बाँगरू) of the Jind district, the core Bangar tract of Haryana, as the author's mother tongue and treats Bangru as a dialect of Haryanvi; Glottolog hary1238 lists Bangaru/Bangri as alternate names, so no separate glottocode applies. Sharma 1968 describes 'Central Haryanvi' of Meham (Rohtak district) and says only palatalization separates it from the Bangru sub-dialect. Ahmed et al. 2026 concerns the Pakistani Haryanvi (Rangri) diaspora variety.

tone_statements.citation: Sangeeta. 2020. A linguistic insight into Hindi and Haryanvi language. International Journal of Innovations in TESOL and Applied Linguistics (IJITAL) 5(3). 9 pp. Gurgaon: ASLA, Amity University.
tone_statements.quote: Compared to Hindi- Haryanvi has weak but predictable word stress. [...] (In Hindi emphasis is accomplished by higher pitch rather than by the heavier articulation that typifies English.) In Haryanvi high pitch is emphasized same as in the Hindi, change in the tone and higher pitch. The result of this is the sing-song effect that English spoken by Hindi-Haryanvi learners often has on native-English speakers.
tone_statements.locator: (article unpaginated), section on pronunciation differences between Hindi/Haryanvi and English

tone_statements.quote: (क) अतिखंडीय--(Supra-Segmental) (१) सुर (Pitch) उच्च ३ मध्य २ निम्न १ (२) आन्तसुर (Terminal contour) सम > उन्नायक T अवनायक | निम्नोन्नायक- … ३--(१) सुर तथा आन्तसुर : हरियाणवी में ऊपर लिखे अनुसार तीन सुर ओर चार आन्तसुर हैं। इनके संयोग से काकुपद्धति का निर्माण होता है। काकु द्वारा अनेक अर्थों की अभिव्यक्ति होती है। हमारे कथन में किसी विशेष स्थल हे oo सम, उन्नायक, अवनायक अथवा निम्नोन्नायक होना कथन के ऐसे खण्ड को al | करता है जिसे साधारण भाषा में वाक्य कहा जाता है
tone_statements.translation: (a) Suprasegmental: (1) pitch: high 3, mid 2, low 1; (2) terminal contour: level, rising, falling, falling-rising … 3.(1) Pitch and terminal contour: as written above, Haryanvi has three pitches and four terminal contours. From their combination the intonation system (kāku-paddhati) is built. Many meanings are expressed through intonation. At any particular point in our utterance, [the contour] being level, rising, falling or falling-rising [marks off] that stretch of the utterance which in ordinary language is called a sentence.
tone_statements.locator: Dhvani-saṃracnā, prathama khaṇḍa: 'Hariyāṇvī ke dhvanigrām' §2 (क) atikhaṇḍīya, p. 44, and 'Dhvanigrāmoṃ kā vivaraṇ' §3 (1) sur tathā āntasur, p. 45

sources.note: Phoneme inventory of Central Haryanvi (Meham, Rohtak; author's own speech), pp. 44-46: supra-segmental phonemes are (1) sur/pitch with three levels, (2) āntasur/terminal contour (four), (3) juncture, (4) nasality — no stress phoneme is listed and no word-stress placement rule is given. Diachronic chapters use 'svarāghāt' (accent) only to explain loss/shortening of unaccented vowels (e.g. pp. 104, 163); p. 244-ish notes a special emphatic balāghāt on interjections.

tone.translation: (a) Suprasegmental: (1) pitch: high 3, mid 2, low 1; (2) terminal contour: level, rising, falling, falling-rising … 3.(1) Pitch and terminal contour: as written above, Haryanvi has three pitches and four terminal contours.
